title: TMJ, Trunk, Thorax, Pelvis, Hip & Knee
summary: This unit covers the jaw, spine and trunk, thorax and breathing, pelvis, hip and knee: their bones, joints, ligaments, motions and the muscles that move them (origins, insertions, actions, nerves). It also covers common conditions and OT precautions, including the Valsalva maneuver and total hip and knee replacement. It ends with an Exam 3 checklist and highlights from the course-wide comprehensive review.

sections.heading: Temporomandibular Joint (TMJ)
body: The TMJ sits just in front of the ear, where the condyle of the mandible meets the temporal bone. An articular disk sits between them. It is a synovial, hinge-like joint that also glides, and it is one of the most heavily used joints in the body: chewing, talking, yawning and swallowing.
Structure: 2 bones, a disk, a joint capsule, ligaments and 4 main muscles of mastication.
Motions: elevation (close mouth), depression (open mouth), protraction/protrusion (jaw forward), retraction/retrusion (jaw back), lateral deviation (side to side).

MuscleOriginInsertionActionInnervation
TemporalisTemporal fossa of skullCoronoid process and ramus of mandibleElevation; retraction (posterior fibers); unilateral: lateral deviation to the same sideTrigeminal (CN V)
MasseterZygomatic archAngle and ramus of mandibleElevation (strongest closer); assists protraction; unilateral: lateral deviation to the same sideTrigeminal (CN V)
Medial pterygoidMedial surface of lateral pterygoid plate (sphenoid)Medial surface of ramus/angle of mandibleElevation, protraction; unilateral: lateral deviation to the opposite sideTrigeminal (CN V)
Lateral pterygoidGreater wing and lateral pterygoid plate of sphenoidNeck of mandibular condyle and TMJ diskProtraction and depression (opening); unilateral: lateral deviation to the opposite sideTrigeminal (CN V)

Hyoid muscles: suprahyoids (digastric, mylohyoid, geniohyoid, stylohyoid) assist depression of the mandible; infrahyoids (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, omohyoid) stabilize the hyoid and assist swallowing and speech.

Innervation for this region overall involves cranial nerves V (trigeminal), VII (facial) and XII (hypoglossal, carrying C1 fibers to geniohyoid/thyrohyoid); infrahyoids are supplied by the ansa cervicalis (C1-C3).
Functional example: opening your mouth against light resistance = mandibular depression with a concentric contraction of the lateral pterygoid (helped by suprahyoids).
Bones of the head and face to know on models: frontal, parietal, temporal (with mastoid process), sphenoid, occipital (with foramen magnum), nasal, zygomatic, maxilla, mandible.

sections.heading: Vertebral Column: Bones, Curves, Joints and Ligaments
body: The spinal column is the bony housing for the spinal cord. Its functions: hold the body upright, protect the spinal cord, and act as a pivot for movement while supporting the head.

RegionNumberKey features
Cervical7Smallest; bifid spinous processes; transverse foramina for vertebral vessels; includes C1 atlas and C2 axis
Thoracic12Long, downward-pointing spinous processes; facets for the 12 pairs of ribs
Lumbar5Largest bodies; thick, blunt spinous processes
Sacrum5 fusedSeparate at birth, fuse with growth; articulates with ilia at the SI joints
Coccyx~4 fusedTailbone; fuses during growth
Total: about 33 vertebrae. Parts of a typical vertebra: body, vertebral foramen, spinous process, transverse processes, facets.

Four curves: cervical and lumbar are lordotic (convex anteriorly); thoracic and sacral are kyphotic (concave anteriorly). The curves make the column roughly 10x stronger than a straight rod and keep the center of gravity over the base of support.
Abnormal curves: kyphosis = exaggerated thoracic curve; lordosis = exaggerated lumbar curve; scoliosis = lateral curve, usually thoracic.

Joints: intervertebral (facet) joints are small gliding joints, but the column as a whole is triaxial. The atlanto-occipital joint (skull-C1) allows nodding; the atlantoaxial joint (C1-C2) allows most cervical rotation.

Ligaments:
  • Anterior longitudinal - front of vertebral bodies; limits hyperextension
  • Posterior longitudinal - back of bodies inside the canal; limits flexion
  • Supraspinous - tips of spinous processes (continues as ligamentum nuchae in the neck)
  • Interspinous - between spinous processes
  • Ligamentum flavum - connects laminae; elastic, yellow
Motions: flexion, extension, hyperextension, lateral flexion (bending), rotation; the cervical spine also protracts and retracts.

Occupation examples: flexion - writing, tying shoes; extension - standing upright in line; hyperextension - leaning back at a shampoo bowl; lateral bending - putting in ear drops; rotation - turning to look at someone talking.

sections.heading: Muscles of the Neck and Trunk

sections.heading: Thorax: Bones, Joints and Mechanics of Breathing
body: Bones: sternum (manubrium, body, xiphoid process), 12 pairs of ribs, costal cartilages, 12 thoracic vertebrae. The thorax is wider side to side than front to back; it protects the heart, lungs and upper abdominal organs.

Ribs: true ribs 1-7 attach directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilage; false ribs 8-10 attach indirectly through the cartilage of rib 7; floating ribs 11-12 have no anterior attachment. Each rib articulates with 2 thoracic vertebrae.
Joints: costovertebral (rib head to vertebral bodies and rib tubercle to transverse process) and sternocostal joints - both diarthrodial, nonaxial gliding joints.
Motion: ribs glide/rotate up (elevation) and out with inspiration, and down (depression) and in with expiration.
Respiratory tract: upper = nasal cavity, oral cavity, pharynx, larynx; lower = trachea, bronchial tree, alveoli; the pleura is the membrane sac around each lung.

Pressure principle: the lungs are passive. Air moves from higher to lower pressure. When the thorax enlarges, pressure inside drops and air flows in; when it gets smaller, pressure rises and air flows out.
Two ways to change thoracic volume: move the ribs, or lower the diaphragm. The diaphragm and intercostals are the most important respiratory muscles.

Diaphragmatic vs chest breathing: diaphragmatic breathing is the most efficient (belly moves out as the diaphragm drops). Chest breathing recruits rib cage and shoulder girdle muscles, costs more energy, is faster and raises the risk of hyperventilation. Gravity helps the diaphragm descend, so elevate the head of the bed for a client with breathing difficulty.

sections.heading: Phases of Respiration, Respiratory Muscles and the Valsalva Maneuver
body:
PhaseWhenMuscles
Quiet inspirationAt restDiaphragm, external intercostals
Deep inspirationNeed more airQuiet muscles + SCM, scalenes, pectoralis major (reverse action), levator costarum, serratus posterior superior
Forced inspirationAir hungerAll of the above + levator scapulae, upper trapezius, rhomboids, pectoralis minor (reverse actions; shoulder girdle lifted)
Quiet expirationAt restPassive: relaxation of diaphragm/external intercostals, elastic recoil, gravity (internal intercostals may assist)
Forced expirationCoughing, blowing, exertionInternal intercostals, abdominals (rectus abdominis, external/internal obliques, transverse abdominis), quadratus lumborum, serratus posterior inferior

MuscleOriginInsertionActionInnervation
DiaphragmXiphoid, inner surfaces of lower 6 ribs/costal cartilages, L1-L3 vertebrae (crura)Central tendonContracts and descends to enlarge the thorax vertically - prime mover of inspirationPhrenic nerve (C3-C5)
External intercostalsInferior border of rib aboveSuperior border of rib below (fibers run down and forward)Elevate ribs - inspirationIntercostal nerves (T1-T11)
Internal intercostalsSuperior border of rib belowInferior border of rib above (fibers run down and back)Depress ribs - forced expirationIntercostal nerves (T1-T11)

Valsalva maneuver: attempting to exhale against a closed glottis. It raises intrathoracic and intra-abdominal pressure, which stabilizes the spine during heavy effort but impedes venous return to the heart and causes swings in heart rate and blood pressure. Risky for clients with cardiovascular compromise. It can happen during lifting, straining with bowel movements, childbirth pushing, repositioning in bed, coughing or sneezing.
OTA takeaway: coach clients to breathe out slowly during exertion and never hold their breath during exercise.

Common respiratory conditions:
  • URI - nose, throat, larynx (cold, flu, laryngitis, hay fever)
  • Lower respiratory infection/disease - trachea to alveoli (pneumonia, bronchitis, emphysema, asthma)
  • Hyperventilation - rapid breathing blowing off too much CO2
  • Stitch - diaphragm cramp below the ribs; hiccups - involuntary diaphragm spasms
  • Pleurisy - inflamed pleura; pneumothorax - collapsed lung
  • Flail chest - multiple rib fractures; chest wall moves in on inspiration and out on expiration (paradoxical)
  • Asthma - bronchial spasm making exhalation especially hard

sections.heading: The Pelvic Girdle
body: Bones: two hip (coxal) bones - each formed by the fused ilium, ischium and pubis - plus the sacrum and coccyx. Landmarks: iliac crest, iliac fossa, ASIS, PSIS, ischial tuberosity (sitting bone), pubic symphysis, obturator foramen, acetabulum.

Functions: supports upper-body weight transmitted down the spine and passes it to the hips; receives ground reaction forces and directs them up to the spine; supports and protects pelvic organs; provides muscle attachments; forms the bony birth canal; plays a central role in posture, balance and musculoskeletal alignment.

False pelvis (greater/major) = superior portion between the iliac wings, no pelvic organs. True pelvis (lesser/minor) = inferior portion containing GI, urinary and reproductive organs and the birth canal.
Joints: pubic symphysis (fibrocartilage disk, amphiarthrosis); sacroiliac (SI) joint - synovial, nonaxial, between sacrum and ilium, very stable with little mobility; lumbosacral joint - L5 on S1.

SI motion: small, debated rotation/translation; increases in pregnancy and decreases with age. Nutation = sacral flexion (top of sacrum moves anterior/inferior, coccyx moves posterior). Counternutation = sacral extension (top moves posterior/superior, coccyx moves anterior).

Lumbosacral joint: has two extra ligaments (iliolumbar and lumbosacral). Optimal lumbosacral angle is about 30 degrees; a larger angle increases shear stress on the joint and disk and is a common source of low back pain.

Pelvic motionLumbar spineHip
Anterior tilt (ASIS moves forward/down, ahead of pubic symphysis)Hyperextension (increased lordosis)Flexion
Posterior tiltFlexion (flattened lumbar curve)Extension
Lateral tilt (unsupported side drops)Lateral flexion toward the weight-bearing sideWeight-bearing hip adducts; non-weight-bearing hip abducts
Forward rotation (non-stance side moves forward)Rotation to the opposite sideWeight-bearing hip medially rotates
Backward rotationRotation to the opposite sideWeight-bearing hip laterally rotates

Force couples: anterior tilt = trunk extensors (erector spinae) + hip flexors (iliopsoas, rectus femoris). Posterior tilt = trunk flexors (rectus abdominis, obliques) + hip extensors (gluteus maximus, hamstrings). Hiking the unsupported side = quadratus lumborum on that side + hip abductors (gluteus medius) on the weight-bearing side.

Habitual postureTrunk extensors & hip flexorsTrunk flexors & hip extensors
Anterior pelvic tiltShortened (tight)Lengthened (weak)
Posterior pelvic tiltLengthenedShortened

sections.heading: The Hip Joint: Structure, Motions and Muscles
body: The hip (coxofemoral) joint is a synovial, ball-and-socket, triaxial joint: the femoral head sits in the acetabulum (formed by ilium, ischium and pubis). The deep socket, deepened further by the acetabular labrum, makes it very stable but less mobile than the shoulder. It is essential for weight bearing and walking.
Femur landmarks: head, neck, greater trochanter, lesser trochanter, linea aspera, medial/lateral condyles and epicondyles, patellar surface.

Ligaments: iliofemoral (strongest, Y-ligament, limits hyperextension), pubofemoral, ischiofemoral, all reinforcing the cylindrical capsule. Inguinal ligament runs from ASIS to pubic tubercle, separating the abdominal wall from the thigh (femoral vessels and nerve pass beneath). Iliotibial band (tract) is the long tendon of the TFL (and part of gluteus maximus) running down the lateral thigh to the lateral tibia.

MotionNormal ROM
Flexion0-120 degrees
Hyperextension0-30 degrees
Abduction0-45 degrees
Adduction0-30 degrees (past neutral)
Internal (medial) rotation0-45 degrees
External (lateral) rotation0-45 degrees
Grouping by location: anterior = flexors; posterior = extensors (and lateral rotators); medial = adductors; lateral = abductors.

Reverse action of gluteus medius/minimus: when standing on one leg, they hold the pelvis level so the opposite side does not drop. Weakness produces a Trendelenburg sign/gait (pelvis drops on the unsupported side).

Strengthening and stretching: to strengthen concentrically, perform the prime motion against resistance applied in the opposite direction; eccentric strengthening = controlled lengthening against resistance (lowering); isometric = contraction without joint movement. To stretch a muscle, move the joint(s) opposite to every prime action (e.g., stretch iliopsoas with hip extension).

Functional notes: a raised toilet seat reduces the hip flexion needed to sit and stand. Standing with feet apart, knees together and pushing down on the knees places the hips in adduction and internal rotation.

sections.heading: Hip Pathologies, Fractures and Total Hip Replacement
body:
• Congenital hip dislocation - AKA developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH); a shallow acetabulum lets the femoral head slide up and stretch the capsule.
  • Legg-Calve-Perthes disease - AKA coxa plana; avascular necrosis of the femoral head followed by revascularization and repair over 2-4 years; mostly boys about 4-10 years old.
  • Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE) - in adolescents during the growth spurt, the proximal femoral epiphysis slips off the femoral neck.
  • Osteoarthritis of the hip - degeneration of the articular cartilage from trauma and wear and tear of aging; often treated with THR/THA.
  • Hip fractures - femoral neck (intracapsular) or intertrochanteric (extracapsular); common in older adults, especially women with osteoporosis. Signs: shortened, externally rotated leg, inability to bear weight, pain that may refer to the knee.
  • Iliotibial band syndrome - overuse friction of the IT band over the lateral femoral epicondyle with repeated knee flexion/extension (runners, cyclists); lateral knee pain.
  • Trochanteric bursitis - inflammation of the bursa over the greater trochanter from repetitive stress/overuse.
  • Hamstring strain - pulled hamstring; the most common muscle strain and frequently recurrent; overload during sprinting.
  • Hip pointer - severe bruise of the iliac crest.

Fractures in general: complete vs incomplete (greenstick), open (compound - skin broken, higher infection risk) vs closed, comminuted (multiple fragments). Healing stages: hematoma, inflammation, fibrocartilaginous callus (2-6 weeks), bony callus/union, remodeling (6 weeks-1 year). Complications include infection, compartment syndrome, fat emboli, nerve damage, delayed union, malunion and nonunion. Treatment: immobilization, closed or open reduction (ORIF with pins, plates, screws), traction. Falls are the leading cause of fractures in older adults; about 1 in 5 people die within a year after hip fracture, and clients who receive OT return to independence sooner.

Total hip replacement (THR) / total hip arthroplasty (THA): replaces the acetabulum and femoral head with implants (cemented or cementless; cementless needs stricter precautions, often younger clients). Indicated for severe pain/deterioration from OA, RA, certain fractures, avascular necrosis or tumors, usually in people about 60+. Implants last roughly 10-25 years.

Posterior/posterolateral approach precautions (typically 6-8 weeks): no hip flexion past 90 degrees, no internal rotation of the operated leg, no adduction past midline (sleep with an abduction wedge/pillow). Anterior approach: avoid hip extension and external rotation. Weight-bearing precautions are common. No driving for about 4-6 weeks.

OT role: clients need adaptive equipment (reacher, sock aid, long-handled sponge/shoe horn, raised toilet seat) to follow precautions and be independent with dressing and toileting; many facilities run pre-op education classes.

sections.heading: The Knee Joint: Structure, Motions and Muscles
body: The tibiofemoral joint is the largest joint in the body: a synovial, modified hinge. It has little bony stability and depends on ligaments and muscles, making it one of the most complex and frequently injured joints. Rotation is an accessory motion; it happens because the medial femoral condyle is longer than the lateral (the basis of the 'screw-home' locking in full extension).
Bones: femur, tibia and patella (the fibula is not part of the knee joint proper but is attached via the LCL and biceps femoris).
ROM: flexion 0-135 degrees; extension returns to 0 (a few degrees of hyperextension is possible but not a normal goal).

LigamentLocation / role
ACL - anterior cruciateInside the joint; prevents the tibia sliding forward on the femur
PCL - posterior cruciateInside the joint; prevents the tibia sliding backward on the femur
MCL - medial (tibial) collateralMedial side; resists valgus (inward-knee) force
LCL - lateral (fibular) collateralLateral side, femur to fibular head; resists varus force

Menisci: medial and lateral C-shaped (half-moon) wedges of fibrocartilage on the tibial plateau; thicker at the outer edge, they deepen the flat tibial surface and absorb shock. The knee also has about 13 bursae to reduce tendon friction.

Popliteal space: area behind the knee bordered by the hamstrings and gastrocnemius; contains nerves and vessels. Pes anserine ('goose foot') = sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus inserting together on the proximal anteromedial tibia.

Patellofemoral joint: the patella is the largest sesamoid bone, embedded in the quadriceps tendon. It increases the leverage (mechanical advantage) of the quadriceps in extension, stabilizes the anterior knee in flexion and protects the joint.
Tibiofibular joints: proximal and distal, like the radius/ulna; small gliding joints joined by an interosseous membrane.

Q angle: angle between the line of pull of the quadriceps (ASIS to mid-patella) and the patellar tendon (mid-patella to tibial tuberosity). Normal is about 13 degrees in males and 18 degrees in females (roughly 13-18). A larger angle increases lateral pull on the patella and is linked to patellofemoral problems.

MuscleOriginInsertionActionInnervation
Rectus femorisAIISTibial tuberosity via patellar tendonKnee extension; hip flexion (2-joint)Femoral nerve (L2-L4)
Vastus lateralis, medialis, intermediusFemur (greater trochanter/linea aspera; anterior shaft for intermedius)Tibial tuberosity via patellar tendonKnee extension (1-joint)Femoral nerve (L2-L4)
Hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris)Ischial tuberosity (biceps short head: linea aspera)Medial tibia / fibular headKnee flexion; hip extension (except short head)Sciatic nerve (L5-S2)
GastrocnemiusMedial and lateral femoral condylesCalcaneus via Achilles tendonKnee flexion; ankle plantar flexion (2-joint)Tibial nerve (S1-S2)
PopliteusLateral femoral condylePosterior proximal tibia'Unlocks' the extended knee by medially rotating the tibia (laterally rotating femur) to start flexionTibial nerve (L4-S1)
Sartorius, gracilis and TFL also cross the knee (sartorius/gracilis flex; TFL stabilizes laterally via the IT band).

Active insufficiency: a 2-joint muscle cannot shorten enough to produce full motion at both joints at once. Hamstrings extend the hip and flex the knee; with the hip already extended they run out of contraction before full knee flexion. Working hamstrings with the hip slightly flexed keeps them lengthened at the hip and is more effective for strengthening.

sections.heading: Knee Pathologies and Total Knee Replacement
body:
• Genu valgum - knock-knees; the lower leg angles laterally (knees touch).
  • Genu varum - bowlegs; the lower leg angles medially.
  • Genu recurvatum - back knees; hyperextension of the knee.
  • Patellar tendonitis - jumper's knee; tenderness at the patellar tendon/inferior pole of the patella from repetitive jumping.
  • Osgood-Schlatter disease - overuse of the quadriceps in growing adolescents causes painful inflammation/bony bump at the tibial tuberosity.
  • Baker's cyst - popliteal cyst; synovial herniation or bursitis in the back of the knee.
  • Patellofemoral pain syndrome - runner's knee; diffuse anterior knee pain, often linked to Q angle, patella alta, quad weakness/tightness or excessive foot pronation.
  • Chondromalacia patella - softening and breakdown of cartilage on the posterior patella; anterior knee pain.
  • Prepatellar bursitis - housemaid's knee; from constant kneeling pressure (e.g., carpet layers).
  • Unhappy triad - single blow to the lateral knee tearing the ACL, MCL and medial meniscus.

Total knee replacement (TKR) / total knee arthroplasty (TKA): usually for severe OA/RA. Immediate post-op: pain control and early mobilization to strengthen the quadriceps and preserve ROM (sometimes a CPM machine). Out of bed in 1-3 days; goals include knee flexion to 90 degrees, full extension and walking with an assistive device.

TKR precautions: no twisting/rotation of the knee, no kneeling, no pillow under the knee in bed (risk of flexion contracture), rest both feet flat on the floor when sitting, wear the immobilizer as ordered; some procedures limit full flexion. Return to normal activities about 3-6 weeks; driving about 4-6 weeks.

sections.heading: Exam 3 Checklist
body: From the instructor's study guide - be ready for multiple choice (some multiple-answer), matching, short answer/fill in the blank, and muscle/prime motion/activity/stretch short answers.

• Prime movers and how muscles group by location (anterior/posterior/medial/lateral)
  • ALL prime motions of each muscle, including assists (needed for stretching)
  • Joint motions and normal hip and knee ROM
  • Pelvic tilts, their muscles, and the matching vertebral and hip motions
  • TMJ motions, muscles and functional use
  • Trunk, head and neck muscles with bilateral vs unilateral actions
  • How to stretch, and concentric vs eccentric vs isometric strengthening
  • Pathologies and precautions: THR, TKR, gout, fractures and highlighted conditions
  • Hindfoot, midfoot, forefoot and the joints of the foot and ankle
  • 1-joint vs 2-joint muscles
  • Q angle
  • Bursa vs ligament vs cartilage (menisci, costal cartilage) vs tendon
  • True vs false pelvis; nutation/counternutation
  • Valsalva maneuver and why it matters
  • Matching ligament names to their joints
  • Respiratory muscles in quiet/deep/forced inspiration and quiet/forced expiration
Tip from the guide: it's fine to move and act out the motions during the test - and breathe!
Note: the foot/ankle and gout items are covered in a separate unit; review them there.

sections.heading: Comprehensive Review Highlights
body:
PlaneDivides body intoMotionsAxis
SagittalLeft and rightFlexion/extensionFrontal (medial-lateral)
Frontal (coronal)Front and backAbduction/adduction, radial/ulnar deviation, inversion/eversionSagittal (anterior-posterior)
Transverse (horizontal)Upper and lowerRotation, supination/pronation, horizontal abduction/adductionVertical (longitudinal)

Synovial joint types: gliding/plane - nonaxial (carpals); hinge - uniaxial (elbow, knee); pivot - uniaxial (atlantoaxial, radioulnar); ellipsoid/condyloid - biaxial (wrist, MCPs); saddle - biaxial (thumb CMC); ball-and-socket - triaxial (hip, shoulder). More mobility = less stability and vice versa.
Skeletal functions: support, protection, leverage for movement, blood cell production, mineral (calcium) storage.

Pathology terms: fracture (break), dislocation (complete separation of joint surfaces), subluxation (partial dislocation - common at the shoulder after stroke), capsulitis, sprain (ligament), strain (muscle/tendon overstretch), tendonitis.

Nervous system: CNS = brain and spinal cord; PNS = 12 cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves; ANS = sympathetic (fight or flight) and parasympathetic (rest and digest). Gray matter (H shape) - posterior horn sensory, anterior horn motor; white matter = ascending/descending tracts. Pain and temperature tracts cross at the spinal level; most touch/position tracts cross in the brainstem; about 80% of motor fibers cross in the brainstem.

UMN vs LMN: UMN lesions (SCI, MS, CVA, Parkinsonism, TBI) - spasticity, hyperreflexia. LMN lesions (peripheral nerve injury, polio, muscular dystrophy-type conditions, myasthenia gravis listed in class) - flaccidity, hyporeflexia, atrophy. Brown-Sequard syndrome: hemisection of the cord - same-side motor and proprioceptive loss, opposite-side pain and temperature loss.

Shoulder: rotator cuff = SITS (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis). Scapulohumeral rhythm: after the first ~30 degrees, 2 degrees of glenohumeral motion for every 1 degree of scapular upward rotation - mobilize the scapula before ranging a tight shoulder. Full abduction requires external rotation. Common problems: subluxation post-CVA, impingement, adhesive capsulitis, rotator cuff tear.

Elbow and forearm: elbow = humeroulnar/humeroradial hinge, 0-150 degrees, MCL/LCL; hyperextension blocked by the olecranon in the olecranon fossa. Radioulnar = pivot; supination 0-80/85, pronation 0-70/80; the radius moves around the ulna.

Wrist and hand: radiocarpal = condyloid, biaxial (radius with scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum; ulna excluded by the articular disk); flexion 0-80, extension 0-70, radial deviation 0-20, ulnar deviation 0-30. Functional hand position: wrist slightly extended, MCP/PIP slightly flexed, thumb opposed. Safe (intrinsic-plus) position: wrist extended, MCPs flexed, IPs extended. Arches: proximal and distal transverse, longitudinal. Grasps: cylindrical, spherical, hook, intrinsic plus; precision: tip, palmar (three-jaw chuck), lateral (key) pinch.

UE nerves: the brachial plexus is formed by C5-T1. Radial nerve (posterior cord) - dorsal hand/thumb side, wrist and finger extensors; median nerve (lateral + medial cords) - palmar thumb, index, middle, half of ring; ulnar nerve (medial cord) - ring and little fingers.

Final exam reminders: comprehensive; knee flexors; knee is the most frequently injured joint; forefoot/midfoot/hindfoot; brachial vs lumbosacral plexus; PAD/DAB (palmar interossei adduct, dorsal abduct) applies to hand and foot; contracting the right SCM rotates the head to the left; parts of the pelvis; hip, knee and ankle ROM; which ligaments belong to which joint.

terms.def: Synovial hinge-like joint with gliding between the mandibular condyle and temporal bone, with an articular disk.
Side-to-side movement of the mandible.
Moving the jaw forward.
Strongest jaw-closing muscle, from zygomatic arch to mandible angle; CN V.
Muscle that protracts and depresses the mandible and deviates it to the opposite side.
Digastric, mylohyoid, geniohyoid, stylohyoid; assist mandibular depression.
Anterior-convex spinal curve (normal in cervical/lumbar); also the term for an exaggerated lumbar curve.
Posterior-convex curve (normal thoracic/sacral); abnormal when the thoracic curve is exaggerated.
Abnormal lateral curvature of the spine, usually thoracic.
First two cervical vertebrae; atlantoaxial joint provides most neck rotation.
Elastic yellow ligament connecting the laminae of adjacent vertebrae.
Runs along the front of vertebral bodies; limits hyperextension.
Neck muscle: bilateral flexion; unilateral lateral flexion same side and rotation to opposite side; CN XI.
Deep back group (semispinalis, multifidus, rotatores); unilateral rotation to the opposite side.
Iliocostalis, longissimus, spinalis; prime trunk extensors.
Lateral trunk muscle that laterally flexes the trunk and hikes the hip.
Ribs 1-7, attaching directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilage.
Ribs 8-10, attaching to the sternum through the cartilage of rib 7.
Ribs 11-12, with no anterior attachment.
Gliding joint where a rib meets thoracic vertebral bodies and transverse process.
Efficient breathing driven by diaphragm descent; abdomen moves out.
Dome muscle; prime mover of inspiration; phrenic nerve C3-C5.
Elevate the ribs during inspiration.
Depress the ribs during forced expiration.
Inspiration during air hunger using shoulder girdle muscles in reverse action.
Exhaling against a closed glottis; raises intrathoracic pressure and stresses the heart.
Multiple rib fractures causing paradoxical chest wall movement.
Collapsed lung from air in the pleural space.
Inferior (lesser) pelvis containing pelvic organs and the birth canal.
Superior (greater) pelvis between the iliac wings; no pelvic organs.
Sacral flexion: top of sacrum moves anteriorly, coccyx posteriorly.
Sacral extension: top of sacrum moves posteriorly, coccyx anteriorly.
ASIS moves forward/down; accompanies lumbar hyperextension and hip flexion.
Two muscle groups pulling in different directions to produce one rotation (e.g., pelvic tilt).
Anterior superior iliac spine; origin of sartorius and TFL.
Hip socket formed by the ilium, ischium and pubis.
Fibrocartilage rim that deepens the acetabulum.
Strong Y-shaped anterior hip ligament limiting hyperextension.
Runs from ASIS to pubic tubercle; separates the abdominal wall from the thigh.
Long tendon of TFL running down the lateral thigh to the lateral tibia.
Pelvis drops on the unsupported side due to weak hip abductors on the stance side.
Muscle lengthens while producing force, e.g., slowly lowering a load.
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children (coxa plana).
Slipped capital femoral epiphysis; epiphysis slips off the femoral neck in adolescents.
Replacement of acetabulum and femoral head with implants.
Open reduction internal fixation: surgical alignment with pins, plates or screws.
Raised pressure within a fascial compartment compressing nerves and vessels.
C-shaped fibrocartilage disks on the tibia that deepen the joint and absorb shock.
Anterior cruciate ligament; prevents anterior tibial translation.
Shared insertion of sartorius, gracilis and semitendinosus on the medial tibia.
Angle between quadriceps line of pull and patellar tendon; about 13-18 degrees.
A 2-joint muscle cannot shorten enough to complete motion at both joints at once.
Small posterior knee muscle that unlocks the knee to begin flexion.
Knock-knees.
Bowlegs.
Combined tear of ACL, MCL and medial meniscus.
Painful inflammation at the tibial tuberosity in adolescents from quadriceps overuse.
About 2 degrees of glenohumeral motion for every 1 degree of scapular rotation.
Cord hemisection: ipsilateral motor loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss.
Crossing of nerve tracts to the opposite side.

questions.q: Which bones form the temporomandibular joint?
questions.explain: The mandibular condyle articulates with the temporal bone, with a disk between.

questions.q: A client opens their mouth against light resistance. Which motion and contraction is occurring?
questions.explain: Opening is depression and the lateral pterygoid/suprahyoids shorten against resistance.

questions.q: Unilateral contraction of the medial pterygoid deviates the mandible toward which side?
choices: It does not deviate the jaw
questions.explain: Both pterygoids deviate the jaw to the opposite side; temporalis and masseter to the same side.

questions.q: Which cranial nerve supplies the four muscles of mastication?
questions.explain: The mandibular branch of CN V innervates temporalis, masseter and both pterygoids.

questions.q: Which muscle is the main protractor of the mandible and also assists opening?
questions.explain: The lateral pterygoid pulls the condyle and disk forward.

questions.q: How many vertebrae are in the cervical, thoracic and lumbar regions?
questions.explain: There are 7 cervical, 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar vertebrae.

questions.q: A bifid spinous process and transverse foramina identify which vertebrae?
questions.explain: Only cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina and typically bifid spines.

questions.q: An exaggerated lateral curve of the spine, usually thoracic, is called:
questions.explain: Scoliosis is a lateral curvature.

questions.q: Which ligament runs along the front of the vertebral bodies and limits hyperextension?
questions.explain: The ALL lies anteriorly and resists backward bending.

questions.q: Putting ear drops into your right ear while seated mainly uses which neck motion?
questions.explain: Tilting the ear toward the shoulder is lateral flexion (bending).

questions.q: To rotate the head to the LEFT, which sternocleidomastoid contracts?
questions.explain: Unilateral SCM rotates the head to the opposite side.

questions.q: Which abdominal muscle rotates the trunk to the SAME side when contracting unilaterally?
questions.explain: Internal oblique rotates to the same side; external oblique to the opposite side.

questions.q: Which trunk muscle compresses the abdomen but produces no trunk motion?
questions.explain: Transverse abdominis fibers run horizontally and act like a corset.

questions.q: A client with a stiff knee hikes the hip to clear the foot when walking. Which muscle is the primary hip hiker?
questions.explain: Quadratus lumborum elevates the pelvis on the same side.

questions.q: Unilateral contraction of the transversospinalis group rotates the trunk:
questions.explain: Transversospinalis (e.g., multifidus, rotatores) rotates to the opposite side.

questions.q: Ribs 8-10 are classified as:
questions.explain: They attach indirectly to the sternum via rib 7's cartilage.

questions.q: What happens to pressure inside the lungs during inspiration?
choices: It decreases, so air flows out
It increases, so air flows in
It decreases, so air flows in
questions.explain: Enlarging the thorax lowers internal pressure; air moves toward lower pressure.

questions.q: Why should you elevate the head of the bed for a client with breathing difficulty?
choices: It prevents the Valsalva maneuver entirely
questions.explain: Gravity pulls abdominal contents down so the diaphragm can drop more easily.

questions.q: Which muscles work during QUIET inspiration?
questions.explain: Quiet inspiration needs only the diaphragm and external intercostals.

questions.q: Quiet expiration is mainly:
choices: Passive - relaxation, elastic recoil and gravity
questions.explain: No active muscle contraction is required at rest.

questions.q: A client in respiratory distress is lifting their shoulders with each breath. Which phase is this?
questions.explain: Air hunger recruits upper trapezius, levator scapulae and others in reverse action.

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the diaphragm?
questions.explain: 'C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive.'

questions.q: Which group is used in FORCED expiration?
questions.explain: These muscles pull the ribs down and push the diaphragm up.

questions.q: The Valsalva maneuver is best described as:
choices: Attempting to exhale against a closed glottis
questions.explain: Closing the glottis while straining raises thoracic pressure.

questions.q: Why do OTAs coach clients to breathe out during exertion?
choices: To avoid the Valsalva maneuver and its cardiovascular stress
questions.explain: Breath holding raises pressure and strains the heart.

questions.q: Chest wall moving inward on inspiration after several fractured ribs describes:
questions.explain: Paradoxical movement is the hallmark of flail chest.

questions.q: The true pelvis is:
choices: The superior portion between the iliac wings
The inferior portion containing pelvic organs and the birth canal
questions.explain: The lesser pelvis lies below the pelvic brim and holds organs.

questions.q: Nutation of the sacrum refers to:
choices: Sacral flexion - top moves anteriorly, coccyx posteriorly
questions.explain: Nutation = sacral flexion.

questions.q: An anterior pelvic tilt is accompanied by:
questions.explain: Tipping the pelvis forward increases lordosis and flexes the hips.

questions.q: Which force couple produces a POSTERIOR pelvic tilt?
questions.explain: Abdominals pull the pubis up while glutes/hamstrings pull the ischium down.

questions.q: A person with a habitual anterior pelvic tilt likely has:
choices: Long hip flexors and trunk extensors
Short hip flexors and trunk extensors, long abdominals and hip extensors
questions.explain: The muscles producing the tilt become shortened.

questions.q: The optimal lumbosacral angle is about:
questions.explain: Larger angles increase shear stress and low back pain.

questions.q: The hip joint is classified as:
questions.explain: The femoral head in the acetabulum moves in three planes.

questions.q: Normal hip flexion ROM is:
questions.explain: The course standard is 0-120 degrees.

questions.q: Which muscle is the prime mover for hip flexion and inserts on the lesser trochanter?
questions.explain: Psoas major and iliacus share an insertion on the lesser trochanter.

questions.q: Which muscle flexes, abducts and laterally rotates the hip AND flexes the knee?
questions.explain: Sartorius produces the 'figure-4' sitting position.

questions.q: Weakness of the gluteus medius produces:
choices: Trendelenburg gait - pelvis drops on the unsupported side
questions.explain: Gluteus medius holds the pelvis level in single-leg stance.

questions.q: The hip adductor group is mainly innervated by the:
questions.explain: The medial thigh is the obturator nerve's territory.

questions.q: To stretch the iliopsoas, you would position the hip in:
questions.explain: Stretch a muscle by moving opposite its prime action.

questions.q: Slowly lowering the leg back down after a straight-leg raise works the hip flexors:
questions.explain: The flexors lengthen while controlling the descent.

questions.q: After a posterior-approach THR, which activity violates precautions?
choices: Bending forward to pick up a shoe from the floor
Using a reacher to retrieve items
Sitting on a raised toilet seat
questions.explain: Bending to the floor flexes the hip past 90 degrees.

questions.q: Typical posterior-approach THR precautions include all EXCEPT:
choices: Encourage crossing the legs when seated
No internal rotation of the operated leg
questions.explain: Crossing the legs causes adduction, which risks dislocation.

questions.q: For an ANTERIOR-approach THR, which motion is typically restricted?
questions.explain: The anterior approach disrupts anterior tissues, so extension/ER are limited.

questions.q: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is:
choices: Slipping of the femoral epiphysis in adolescents
Avascular necrosis of the femoral head in children
A shallow acetabulum present at birth
questions.explain: LCP (coxa plana) mostly affects boys about 4-10.

questions.q: A 'hip pointer' is a bruise of the:
questions.explain: Hip pointers are contusions of the iliac crest.

questions.q: Which muscles form the pes anserine?
questions.explain: Remember 'Say Grace before Tea' (SGT).

questions.q: The ACL primarily prevents:
choices: Anterior translation of the tibia on the femur
questions.explain: The anterior cruciate stops the tibia sliding forward.

questions.q: Normal knee flexion ROM is about:
questions.explain: Typical knee flexion is 0-135 degrees.

questions.q: Which muscle 'unlocks' the fully extended knee to begin flexion?
questions.explain: Popliteus rotates tibia/femur to unlock the screw-home position.

questions.q: Which quadriceps muscle also crosses the hip?
questions.explain: Rectus femoris originates on the AIIS; the vasti arise from the femur.

questions.q: The main function of the patella is to:
choices: Increase the quadriceps' leverage for knee extension
Act as the knee's main ligament
Absorb shock between femur and tibia
questions.explain: As a sesamoid bone it improves the mechanical advantage of the quads.

questions.q: Hamstrings become actively insufficient when the hip is:
choices: Flexed while the knee is flexed
Flexed while the knee is extended
Extended while the knee is flexed
questions.explain: They are shortened over both joints at once.

questions.q: For more effective hamstring strengthening in knee flexion, position the hip in:
questions.explain: Hip flexion keeps the hamstrings lengthened at the hip so they can shorten at the knee.

questions.q: A normal Q angle is approximately:
questions.explain: About 13 degrees in males and 18 in females.

questions.q: Genu valgum is also known as:
questions.explain: In valgum the knees angle in and lower legs out.

questions.q: A single blow to the lateral knee tearing the ACL, MCL and medial meniscus is the:
questions.explain: These three structures are often injured together.

questions.q: An adolescent athlete has a painful bump at the tibial tuberosity. The most likely condition is:
questions.explain: Quadriceps traction at the growth plate of the tibial tuberosity.

questions.q: A carpet layer develops swelling over the front of the kneecap. This is:
questions.explain: Constant kneeling pressure inflames the prepatellar bursa.

questions.q: Which is a standard TKR precaution?
choices: Keep the knee flexed at all times
Do not place a pillow under the knee in bed
questions.explain: A pillow encourages a flexion contracture.

questions.q: Flexion and extension occur in which plane, around which axis?
questions.explain: Flexion/extension occur in the sagittal plane about a medial-lateral axis.

questions.q: Shoulder internal and external rotation occur in which plane?
questions.explain: Rotations occur in the transverse plane around a vertical axis.

questions.q: Which joint is a biaxial saddle joint?
questions.explain: The first carpometacarpal is the classic saddle joint.

questions.q: A partial dislocation, common at the shoulder after a stroke, is a:
questions.explain: Subluxation is incomplete separation of joint surfaces.

questions.q: Which condition is an UPPER motor neuron lesion?
questions.explain: CVA damages neurons in the brain, above the anterior horn.

questions.q: In Brown-Sequard syndrome, pain and temperature are lost on which side?
questions.explain: Spinothalamic fibers cross at the spinal level, so loss is contralateral.

questions.q: The posterior horn of spinal cord gray matter carries:
questions.explain: Sensory in posterior, motor out anterior.

questions.q: Scapulohumeral rhythm after the first 30 degrees is approximately:
choices: 2 degrees of shoulder motion to 1 degree of scapular rotation
questions.explain: The glenohumeral joint moves twice as much as the scapula.

questions.q: Which muscle is NOT part of the rotator cuff?
questions.explain: The cuff is SITS: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis.

questions.q: Elbow hyperextension is normally blocked by:
choices: The olecranon process fitting into the olecranon fossa
questions.explain: Bony contact limits extension; hyperextension suggests ligament laxity.

questions.q: The 'safe' (intrinsic-plus) position of the hand is:
choices: Wrist extended, MCPs extended, IPs flexed
Wrist extended, MCPs flexed, IPs extended
Wrist flexed, MCPs extended, IPs flexed
questions.explain: This keeps collateral ligaments long and prevents claw deformity.

questions.q: Turning a key in a car ignition uses which grasp?
questions.explain: Thumb pad to the side of the index finger is lateral pinch.

questions.q: The brachial plexus is formed from which spinal levels?
questions.explain: The brachial plexus arises from ventral rami C5-T1.

questions.q: Which nerve supplies sensation to the palmar thumb, index and middle fingers?
questions.explain: The median nerve covers the radial 3.5 digits on the palm.

questions.q: The radiocarpal joint does NOT include the ulna because:
choices: The ulna fuses with the radius
An articular disk separates the ulna from the carpals
The ulna is too short to reach the wrist
The ulna articulates only with the humerus
questions.explain: The triangular disk acts as a shock absorber between ulna and carpals.
